slides.title: Game Forge V2 — Help
slides.html: Game Forge V2 fuses the Prompt Gallery (a curated library of build prompts you can run and compare) with the Tool Calling Lab (an agentic loop that writes real files). Here the model builds a complete, multi-file game project — then you run, rate, and compare the results.

slides.title: The app
slides.html: This is the app as it opens. Every screenshot in this deck is captured from the running app, not drawn by hand.

slides.title: Setup
slides.html:
1. Pick a provider/model. Every in-app model build uses the multi-file tool workflow. Use the model dropdown; the gear opens provider settings.
  2. Connect a data root (folder icon). Every build is written to disk under <root>/game-forge-v2/projects/<game>/<runId>/ — nothing is ever overwritten. New run folders begin with the local start date and time (YYYY-MM-DD_HH-mm-ss), keep their unique run ID, and end with a short model name (or the CLI agent plus default when no model was selected). Existing folders still open normally.
  3. Open Budgets before a build if you want to change the hard limits for turns, agent time, idle time, files, bytes, images, tokens, cost, or native validation.

slides.title: Library
slides.html:
• Browse curated game prompts, from 1980 arcade classics to modern indies. The catalogue is split into stable primary categories, with independent filters for collection, target stack, tag, library and kind (originals only, variants only, or both). Search composes with every facet, so "every Three.js variant" or "every original that provisions Phaser" is two clicks.
  • Categories and collections are registered in data/categories.json. New and edited prompts store category, subcategory and collections explicitly; existing seed and custom prompts receive backwards-compatible inferred values.
  • Each card shows the target stack and a "watch for" note — the mechanics a lazy implementation tends to skip.
  • New prompt adds your own. Custom prompts and visibility state are kept in the connected data root; older browser-only prompts migrate automatically.
  • Use the pencil on any card to Save new version. Editing a curated seed adopts it into your library: the curated wording becomes version 1 and your change lands on top as version 2, so data/library.json in the repository is never rewritten and the original is always recoverable from the version list. Earlier versions stay in the library document, and every run pins the exact version and prompt text it used.
  • The bin icon hides a prompt; it never deletes one. Every version stays on disk, a bar above the grid lists what is hidden, and one click restores it — hiding a prompt with variants leaves the variants reachable in the meantime.
  • Import / Export moves the complete custom library, including versions and hidden state, as a portable JSON file. Curated seeds are never modified.
  • Guided prompt wizard is the default because you do not need to understand prompt engineering. Describe the game in plain English, choose who should draft it, then review ordinary editable fields before saving.
  • Drafter choices include the local Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity CLIs, with a searchable optional CLI-model field. Agent jobs use the path-jailed local bridge, a short budget, and append-only <data-root>/game-forge-v2/prompt-drafts/ request/response records.
  • Provider / local model opens the suite's searchable model selector, including LM Studio, Unsloth Studio, Lemonade, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, OpenRouter, and custom model IDs. This drafting choice remains independent from the model used to build the game.
  • Full editor retains the advanced Draft, Improve, Review, and Watch-for operations plus partial-field application.
  • AI-authored versions record the provider, model, operation, timestamp, and applied scope. The card receives an AI badge and the same provenance is copied into every run's immutable prompt snapshot.
  • Clicking outside the prompt dialog deliberately does nothing. Use Cancel or the close button, so an accidental backdrop click cannot discard the idea.
  • A card that has been built carries a run count badge. It shows that prompt's own runs; a prompt with variants shows 4+2, meaning four of its own and two more across its lanes — variants build into their own folders, so the two numbers are never added together. Click the badge to open that game in Runs. Lane rows in the variant strip carry their own counts.
  • Hit Build to load a game into the Build view.

slides.title: Library (cont.)
slides.html:
Project libraries

The prompt editor and guided wizard can choose one engine/renderer, one physics library and one audio library. Available foundations include p5, Phaser, PixiJS, Three.js, Babylon.js, PlayCanvas, KAPLAY, Kontra and melonJS, with Matter.js, Planck or Rapier physics and Tone.js or Howler audio. Choose None / Vanilla Canvas when a dependency would add more weight than value.

Selections are version-pinned and portable. Before a build starts, Game Forge copies the verified files into that run's own lib/ folder; it never gives a generated game a shared/lib or CDN dependency. File sizes and SHA-256 hashes are checked before and after generation, and the model is not allowed to rewrite Forge-owned runtime files. A conflict stops preparation with a clear failure. The selected versions and integrity evidence are preserved in the prompt snapshot, run metadata and trace.

slides.title: Library (cont.)
slides.html: The Brief & libraries button on the Build screen keeps the technical choice and the written brief together. You can edit the title, prompt and watch-for notes directly. Adapt brief uses the backend and model selected on the Build screen: Claude Code, Codex or Antigravity use their CLI model (including CLI default), while In-app model uses the provider model selected in the toolbar. After changing libraries, Adapt brief offers two AI modes: Preserve concept integrates the runtime without changing the presentation, while Transform concept may make a larger change such as turning a sprite-based game into a Three.js 3D scene. An optional intent box makes that choice explicit.

slides.title: Library (cont.)
slides.html:
Review the field-level before/after diff, then choose Use for this run, Save as variant, or—for a custom prompt—Save new version. Variants are append-only child prompts containing a complete resolved snapshot plus parent, library-change and model provenance. Curated seeds remain immutable. Revisions inherit their source brief and libraries so a repair or fork cannot silently switch its runtime.

Classic-script and ES-module profiles are both supported. The in-app preview handles acyclic static relative module imports; workers, runtime fetches, import.meta assets and cyclic module graphs require serving the exported project locally.

slides.title: VR games for Quest 3
slides.html:
Choose VR · Quest 3 in the Library category bar, or Quest 3 Browser VR in the Collection filter. The collection adds 16 build briefs: archery, underwater submersible exploration, a Beat Saber-inspired rhythm game, an Elite-inspired space cockpit, lunar landing, car racing, flight simulation, tabletop city building, and eight more games to discover. The VR category also includes the existing Half-Life: Alyx brief.

These are prompts for generating games. Each selects the portable Three.js runtime and asks for immersive WebXR, Quest Touch controller input, menus you can use inside the headset, comfort settings, and a keyboard/mouse desktop mode. Build a brief as usual, then playtest the generated result; inclusion in this list does not certify a model's output on a headset.

slides.title: VR games for Quest 3 (cont.)
slides.html:
Open the generated game's index.html on Quest Browser from a trusted HTTPS address, then press Enter VR and accept the browser's request. An ordinary http://192.168.… LAN address is not a secure context for immersive VR. Export the project and serve the complete folder, including lib/, to keep it portable. No native Quest application or PC VR streaming is required by these briefs.

Desktop Preview is useful for checking the basic game loop. For a headset test, prefer the game in its own tab; if using Open in new tab from Preview, keep Forge open while its temporary preview URLs are in use. If Enter VR is unavailable, check HTTPS, headset/browser support and permissions. Test both controllers, in-world pause/restart, seated height and exiting/re-entering VR.

The rhythm game uses original synthesised music and artwork; it is inspired by Beat Saber's mechanics, not the commercial game or its song catalogue. The cockpit game similarly uses its own world and assets.

slides.title: Library variants and lanes
slides.html:
One prompt, built several times against different provisioned libraries, so the effect of the library on the resulting game is visible rather than guessed at.

  • A lane is a named library set — Vanilla Canvas, Phaser, Three.js 3D, Phaser + Howler. Thirteen ship in data/lanes.json; your own live beside the prompt library in the data root and are hidden rather than deleted. A lane is validated by the same rules as any library choice, so it can never name two engines.
  • Vanilla Canvas is a lane like any other, not "the original". A baseline you cannot place in the grid is a baseline you cannot compare against.
  • Create variants in the Library derives one prompt per (game × lane). Pick the games from the current filter, pick the lanes, pick how the text is produced, and the preview tells you the grid size and how many model calls it will cost before you spend anything.

Three ways to produce the variant's text, and they answer different questions:

slides.title: Library variants and lanes (cont.)
slides.html:
Mode What happens Cost
Held constant The prompt text is copied byte for byte; only the provisioned library changes. The library's own constraints still reach the build, because they are injected into the build task rather than the prompt. Free — no model is called
Adapted · preserve The brief is rewritten to use the library while keeping the concept, genre and presentation intent. One model call per cell
Adapted · transform The brief may change presentation substantially — a sprite game can become a 3D scene. Needed for a 2D-worded brief on a 3D lane. One model call per cell

Held constant is the controlled comparison — the one mode where the library really is the only thing that changed. The adapted modes trade that comparability for a brief the library can be good at. Leave Mode on Each lane's default and 2D lanes preserve while 3D lanes transform.

slides.title: Library variants and lanes (cont.)
slides.html:
Variants are ordinary prompts, so they build from the Build screen and through Batch with no special handling, and each lane gets its own runs folder. In the Library they collapse under their parent behind a ⑂ N lanes chip, so the grid keeps its 127 cards; the Lane filter flattens to a single lane across every game ("show me everything built on Phaser"), and Variants as cards restores a flat list.

Re-running a sweep over cells that already exist adds a new prompt version rather than a second prompt — the earlier text stays readable, and ids are deterministic (variant-<game>--<lane>), so a sweep can never duplicate a cell. Every sweep leaves an append-only record in <data-root>/game-forge-v2/library/variant-sweeps/, and every adapted cell also leaves its request and response in brief-reconciliations/.

slides.title: Matrix
slides.html:
The Matrix tab is the payoff: games down the side, lanes across the top, each cell showing that pair's best run — its screenshot, status, and one metric you choose (rubric, files, turns, time or cost). An empty cell offers Build; a row opens up to six lanes side by side with live previews. Runs made before variants existed sit in a Base prompt column and are never attributed to a lane.

Read it carefully, because it will otherwise imply more rigour than it has:

slides.title: Matrix (cont.)
slides.html:
• One run per cell proves nothing. Nondeterminism between two runs of the same cell is routinely larger than the difference between two lanes. Cells show their run count and a single-run cell is labelled provisional.
  • Only held-constant cells are a controlled comparison. An adapted variant differs from its parent in prompt text as well as library.
  • Fewer turns is not better. Phaser supplies scenes, input and physics, so it finishes in fewer turns than Kontra by construction. That measures the library's scope, not the model's competence.
  • The rubric is LLM-judged — a consistent reader, not an objective one, and it has no way to feel whether a game is fun.

The Matrix is an instrument for noticing differences worth looking at by hand. It is not a benchmark table and is deliberately not styled as one.

slides.title: Batch builds
slides.html: Open Batch to run selected games sequentially with the current in-app model or a local Claude Code, Codex or Antigravity CLI. A CLI batch can optionally name a CLI model; leave it empty to use that CLI’s default. Every game remains an independent append-only run with its own trace, budgets and validation evidence. Skip existing matches the complete executor identity. CLI batches require the Hub’s serve.py agent bridge.

slides.title: Build
slides.html:
• Every in-app build is a real multi-file tool build. The model writes the entry point, separate source/style files, README.md, and forge-project.json. Hard stop ends the current run immediately: the in-flight model request is aborted at the socket rather than waited out, and everything already written to the project is kept.
  • Pause / Resume. Next to Hard stop, Pause parks the run without losing anything, and Resume carries on from exactly where it stopped. It is the button for "I want to read the trace before it writes another file", or "stop spending tokens for ten minutes", when a hard stop would be too final.
    • For an in-app model build the pause is cooperative, like the Prompt Gallery's batch runner: the call or tool already in flight is allowed to finish, and the build then parks at the next safe boundary — between two tool calls, or before the next model turn. The banner says Pausing… while it is still finishing, and Paused (with the tool or turn it is about to run next) once nothing is running at all. No new model call is made until you press Resume.
    • For an external CLI agent the bridge suspends the agent's whole process tree with a job-control signal. The agent keeps its context, its files, and its place in the task — it is frozen mid-instruction, not stopped — and continues on Resume. This needs a serve.py new enough to advertise it; if the bridge is older, no Pause button is offered rather than one that cannot work. A caveat: a request the agent had in flight to its model provider can be dropped by that provider while the process is stopped, and the CLI then retries or errors on resume, exactly as it would after any network stall.
    • Paused time is not charged to the run: the trace's elapsed figure excludes it (pausedMs records how long it was parked), and a suspended agent's idle and total-time budgets are held while it sleeps. Every other budget still applies. Pause is per run — a second build started while this one is parked keeps generating — and a Hard stop on a paused run always works: the process is continued first, then stopped. Starting another build while one is parked releases the parked one first, since the Pause button follows the run on screen and a frozen run with no button left is worse than a resumed one.
  • Fresh builds deliberately offer only writing/editing/completion tools. Because the directory starts empty, withholding read_file and list_files prevents small local models from wasting turns inspecting files they just created. Revisions receive both read tools because they must inspect the copied parent.
  • write_file is create-only during a build. An existing path is preserved and the model is directed to use a targeted edit_file call, preventing overwrite loops from repeatedly destroying otherwise-good files.
  • Older tool turns are compacted into status summaries without modifying the original tool arguments. The newest turn remains verbatim. This avoids both context overflow and the local-model failure where a placeholder such as “1.2 KB written” gets copied into the next source file.
  • If a model emits prose instead of a tool call, Game Forge gives it two bounded retries with the exact missing project evidence. A premature report_done is rejected until the manifest, entry point, README, and at least one separate source/style file exist. Conversely, a complete project can finish even when the model forgets the final report_done call.
  • Tool-capable local requests require a tool choice at the API layer. Fresh builds also finish as soon as the host verifies every declared manifest asset and the required multi-file evidence, avoiding a wasteful final model turn.
  • Common local-model argument aliases such as file_path are accepted, fenced JSON and trailing commas are repaired conservatively, and an omitted list_files.path means the project root. Failed calls receive a focused retry instruction instead of encouraging a complete rewrite.
  • The active domain adapter grants only the capabilities needed for this build. Every tool call records its permission, timeout, outcome, duration, and a bounded argument summary in capability-audit.json.
  • Loop detection. Smaller local models often get stuck re-writing the same files instead of finishing. The build watches for this: a turn that only re-writes files with identical content (or churns one file endlessly) counts as "no progress". After a couple of unproductive turns the model gets one nudge to finish or make a real change; if it keeps spinning the build stops early and says so — rather than burning the whole turn budget. The turn cap is now just a safety net, not the main limit. Unproductive turns are badged no progress in the trace, and the telemetry row shows how many redundant rewrites happened.
  • Watching a CLI agent work. Claude Code and Grok stream their partial output, so the agent panel shows a live row of the text, reasoning or file contents being written right now, growing token by token. It is replaced by the ordinary trace row the moment the block completes, and it is never written to trace.jsonl. When the agent is thinking rather than writing, the row shows the thinking-token count instead — extended thinking usually arrives redacted, so the count is the only progress there is, and a five-minute think looks like work rather than a hang. Codex and Antigravity report per-item, so they have no live row.
  • Heal a failed run. When validation fails (or passes with warnings) and the run actually wrote files, the status row grows a Heal button. One click copies the project into a brand-new run and hands the backend the failures the validator recorded, so it repairs rather than rebuilds. The failed run is never modified — its files, trace and evidence stay exactly as they were, so a heal that makes things worse costs you nothing. Heal again on the result to chain attempts. The Runs view's Fix preview does the same thing when you want to add your own guidance first.
  • Reading the trace. Each turn is a collapsible row. Expand it to see the model's text plus, for every tool call, the full Arguments it sent and the Result (or error) it got back — with OK / FAILED badges. If a local model emits malformed argument JSON, the raw text it produced is shown instead of a silent empty call, so you can see exactly why the call failed. A row stays visible while the model call is in flight (calling model…), so a mid-turn API error (e.g. a context-overflow 400) doesn't vanish.
  • Wire inspector (below the trace) shows the raw request/response JSON for any turn — the exact Messages sent, the Request, the raw Response, or the whole trace to Export. Copy or download any of them. This is the fastest way to work out why a model isn't calling tools the way you expect. The full trace is also saved to trace.json in each run folder for later review.
  • The live preview costs something. A generated game runs in the same browser process as Game Forge, so a half-written game with a runaway loop can make the whole page unresponsive. Two things keep that in check: the preview only reboots when the files on disk have actually changed (an agent writing 16 files used to restart the game 16 times; it now restarts once or twice), and the preview bar has a Pause button during a build. Pause keeps whatever is on screen and stops re-running the game — use it the moment the page feels sluggish mid-build. Validation still runs the finished game in its own short-lived frame regardless.
  • When it finishes, the preview boots the project in a sandboxed iframe — a small in-browser file server rewrites the entry index.html's relative links to the built files. Rate the build with the stars.
  • AI assets (checkbox, in-app model only): when on, the build model gets a generate_image tool that renders real sprites / backgrounds / tiles via Wan2GP and saves them into the project as image files it references by relative path. Sprites are generated on a magenta field and the tool keys that out to a transparent PNG. Each image takes several seconds (progress shows in the trace), so the model is told to make only a few key assets. Needs a Wan2GP node configured in media settings.
  • Ask Coach opens the AI mentor (Ask / Quiz / Explain) seeded with the task and a compact project manifest, validation report, runtime errors, recent trace, key source files, and the saved screenshot evidence. Validator and tool-call failures have Explain buttons that open the grounded coach directly.

slides.title: Build (cont.)
slides.html:
Trust status

Finishing generation does not automatically mean a project works. Every run moves through Created → Generating → Stopped → Validating, then receives one of three evidence-based results:

  • Passed — required files, local references, and runtime diagnostics passed.
  • Passed with warnings — the project may work, but has portability, preview-runtime, screenshot, early-stop, or native-verification warnings.
  • Failed validation — required files are missing, local references are broken, the runtime raised errors, or a native build command failed.

Web validation captures console errors, uncaught exceptions, rejected promises, resource-load failures, render dimensions, and preview.png. Native projects use the local bridge to run a restricted stack-specific build check. The full report is saved as validation.json.

Build limits are hard stops rather than suggestions. The remaining budget is shown in the trust panel, and the final budget decision is recorded in forge.json. External-agent limits continue to run in the bridge if the tab is closed.

slides.title: Build (cont.)
slides.html:
No timeout (build bar, or 0 in either time field of the Budgets dialog) removes the two time budgets — the idle timeout and the agent time cap — for builds where no wall-clock number is honest. A local model can spend many minutes on prompt processing before its first token, and killing the turn at that point throws away work that was progressing normally. With it ticked, the turn ends when the model finishes or when you press Hard stop, and nothing else. Every other budget — turns, files, bytes, images, tokens, cost — still applies unchanged, so a runaway build is still bounded.

The setting reaches all the way down: the build loop arms no idle timer, it tells the provider adapter to disable its own stream watchdog (which would otherwise cut in at ten minutes regardless), and the serve.py bridge skips both time checks for external CLI agents. Un-ticking restores the shipped defaults (180s idle, 900s agent time).

slides.title: Build (cont.)
slides.html: For CLI-agent builds the bridge is a separate long-lived process, so the page can easily be newer than the serve.py answering it. An older bridge clamps an unlimited budget up to its ten-second floor — "no timeout" would become the tightest limit in the system. Game Forge therefore asks the bridge what it supports first: if it cannot do unlimited budgets, the run is sent that bridge's maximum instead (2h agent time, 30min idle) and says so in the status row. Restart the hub with serve.py to lift the limit entirely.

slides.title: Improve a finished build
slides.html:
Click Improve beside the rating stars under a finished preview, including a successful build. Enter your own changes, or click Suggest improvements to ask the toolbar's selected model or CLI agent for ideas based on the saved spec, current code excerpts, and available validation results. Suggestions stream as they arrive; Stop suggestions cancels the request.

Completed suggestions are appended to your own instructions. Edit, remove, or add items in Spec additions before clicking Fork & improve. This creates a new run, copies the entire project, and applies the changes to that copy with the normal build budgets, progress, cancellation, and validation. The parent run keeps its files, trace, validation, and rating.

slides.title: Improve a finished build (cont.)
slides.html: The original spec remains in force. Accepted changes are saved as ordered spec additions, alongside the original brief and parent-run link, and carry forward when you improve the child again. AI suggestions become requirements only when you apply the edited instructions. You can also select a saved run in Runs, choose Improve, prepare the changes, and then press Improve copy in Build.

slides.title: Runs
slides.html:
• Every build is saved. Pick a game, then select up to two runs to preview side by side — the same game built by different models, or re-runs of one model.
  • Ratings persist per run.
  • Select one run to use the project-workbench actions:
    • Fork creates an exact new copy without spending a model call.
    • Improve copies the project and prepares a focused model/agent revision.
    • Fix preview attaches the saved validation and runtime failures to a repair task.
    • Continue adds the latest durable trace to the continuation task.
    • Open in agent prepares the copied project for the external coding-agent backend.
  • Select two runs to Diff their full file trees or Merge ideas into a new attempt. The first selected run is the editable base; the second is attached as source/design context.
  • Files / ZIP opens the project browser. Inspect text files, download the complete portable project with vendored fflate, or send all portable text files to Code Morph Lab V3 as an editable local snapshot.
  • Bundle / Port creates an immutable .gameforge.zip contract. A source bundle contains the complete project, creative brief, structured game inventory, validation/evaluation evidence, screenshot, provenance, acceptance criteria and a per-file integrity inventory.
  • Promote to Studio deliberately ends exploration for the selected run and starts a new production lineage. It creates a fresh refinement project every time, copies the run byte-for-byte as an immutable baseline, preserves its validation and screenshot evidence, calculates a baseline SHA-256 inventory, and opens the Refinement Intake audit in a new tab. Promotion never changes or re-runs the source. Failed runs remain failed and show a warning, but can still be promoted when you want a later Studio revision to attempt a repair.
  • A Port handoff bundle adds a reusable target request for Godot, Unity, Unreal Engine, Android native or a desktop wrapper, plus target-agent instructions and a conversion-report template. Game Forge does not claim to translate or compile the game in-browser: a strong agent must work inside the selected target environment, build and run the new project, and return honest mechanic-parity evidence and known gaps.
  • Every bundle export is append-only under <run>/exports/<exportId>/game.gameforge.zip and is downloaded for transfer. Source runs and earlier exports are never overwritten.
  • Evaluate keeps the quick star rating and adds optional 0–5 scores for completeness, playability, visuals, structure, performance, originality, and reliability, plus review notes.
  • Every iteration creates a unique run folder. Its forge.json records parentRunId, sourceRunIds, sourcePromptVersion, iterationKind, and requestedChange; source projects are never overwritten.
  • Run rows show their final validation status. Each run folder preserves forge.json, a compact trace.json, the append-as-it-happens trace.jsonl, validation.json, capability-audit.json, and (for successful browser capture) preview.png.
  • If an external agent survives a reload, Game Forge V2 restores the saved activity and reattaches after the last persisted event.

slides.title: Project manifests and preview adapters
slides.html:
New builds are instructed to write forge-project.json, declaring the project kind, entrypoint, runtime adapter, assets, and controls. Validation checks the declared entry and assets. Older projects remain readable: Game Forge infers an adapter and reports the missing manifest as a warning.

The preview surface now routes through explicit adapters for static web, module-web, workers, WebAssembly, native/archive, and document/data projects. Static web is fully assembled with blob rewriting. Module, worker, and WASM adapters surface their remaining runtime constraints instead of silently pretending every project follows the static-web contract.

slides.title: Record video
slides.html:
Use Record in the toolbar to capture a game preview, build trace, Runs review or any other Forge screen. Chrome lets you choose the current tab, another window or a display and can include supported tab/system audio. The floating controls provide pause, resume and stop before opening a video preview.

Choose MP4 · H.264 for the default upload-friendly output, or WebM when you prefer it. Browsers without native MP4 encoding fall back to WebM automatically.

Download works without a Data Root. With one connected, recordings save append-only under <root>/game-forge-v2/recordings/<recording-id>/, with the current game, run, build lifecycle, backend and model recorded as provenance.

slides.title: Notes & limits
slides.html:
• The previewer targets the web stack (HTML/Canvas/WebGL). It rewrites plain <script src>, <link>, <img> and CSS url() references. ES-module import specifiers, worker URLs, and runtime fetch() of project files are validated but are not yet rewritten; their adapters show a runtime warning.
  • Prompts pinned to non-web stacks (e.g. Doom in C, Elite in Rust) are checked through the local bridge with a restricted stack-specific build command. Without the bridge they are retained with a verification warning.
  • Models must generate art procedurally unless AI assets is enabled — there are no external image/audio assets.
